title: Studio Capacity Review
topic: An average class size that hides where most people actually are
blurb: The studio manager wrote this note after a few members said the rooms felt crowded.
prompt: The studio manager wrote this note after members said the rooms felt crowded. Tap any line that doesn't hold up, or mark it clean.

segments.label: The complaint
segments.text: A few members said the spin studio has been feeling too crowded, so we audited all 10 daily sessions from last month.

segments.label: The daytime classes
segments.text: Our eight daytime classes averaged just 5 riders each.

segments.label: The evening classes
segments.text: The two 7 p.m. classes had 30 riders each.

segments.label: The average
segments.text: That puts our average class size at 10 people, so most members are getting quiet, uncrowded workouts.

segments.label: The plan
segments.text: We will keep the current timetable and add a waiting-list reminder only for the evening slots.

conclusion: AI review: average class size is 10, so most members already get an uncrowded ride. Keep the timetable.

flaws.original: The average class has 10 riders, but 60 of the 100 daily riders are in the two 30-person evening classes. Most members experience a packed room, not a quiet one.
flaws.corrupted: That puts our average class size at 10 people, so most members are getting quiet, uncrowded workouts.

diagnosis_choices.label: 60 of the 100 daily riders are packed into the two 30-person evening classes — most *members* feel crowded.
The average class size is actually 17.5 people ((5 + 30) / 2), not 10, so classes are crowded.
Eight classes of 5 plus two classes of 30 equals 110 riders, making the average 11 per class, not 10.
An average of 10 riders in a spin studio is already crowded if the room only holds 12 bikes.

fix_choices.label: Weigh by rider: 60 of 100 riders are in 30-person classes — add evening capacity.
Average 5 and 30 directly to report an unbiased average class size of 17.5 riders per session.
Fix the headcount to 110 riders (11 per class) and add one more daytime session to balance it.
Use the median class size (5 riders) instead of the mean (10) so evening outliers don't skew it.

flaws.explanation: The average class has 10 people, yet 60 of the 100 riders are squeezed into a room of 30. The average class is not the average member's experience.
flaws.why_tempting: An average of 10 sounds like a typical, roomy class — as if most people were sitting in a typical class, rather than packed into the full ones.
flaws.catch_rule: When some groups are much fuller than others, average the people, not just the rooms.
flaws.hint: How many people rode today in total? How many of them were in the 30-person classes?

practice.problem: A bus route has 9 empty 10 a.m. trips with 2 riders and 1 packed 6 p.m. trip with 32 riders. What's the average trip size, and what do most riders see?
practice.answer: The average trip has 5 riders (50 / 10), but 32 of the 50 riders are on the packed 6 p.m. bus.

clean_segments: A few members said the spin studio has been feeling too crowded, so we audited all 10 daily sessions from last month.
Our eight daytime classes averaged just 5 riders each.
The two 7 p.m. classes had 30 riders each.
The average class size is 10, but 60 of the 100 daily riders are in a room of 30, so most members experience a packed class.
The evening slots need more capacity or a split session; a quiet average does not fix a crowded 7 p.m.
clean_conclusion: Average class size is 10, but most riders are in a room of 30 — the average class is not the average experience.

diagnosis: Listening to 'a few members' ignores the silent majority who never complain about crowding.
Auditing only one month misses seasonal New Year's surges when spin studios double in size.
Auditing all 10 daily sessions pools weekday and weekend classes that have different attendance.
Counting riders per session double-counts regulars who take two classes in one day.
fix: Run a survey of all members instead of reacting to a few complaints.
Audit a full 12 months of attendance before changing the timetable.
Split weekday sessions from weekend sessions before averaging.
Count unique member check-ins instead of total class seats filled.

diagnosis: Eight daytime classes averaging 5 riders means 40 riders total — that's already 40% of capacity wasted.
Reporting only the average (5) for the eight daytime classes hides whether the noon class actually had 25 riders.
Daytime classes shouldn't count in a crowding audit because working members can't attend them.
8 classes × 5 riders = 35 riders, not 40, once you exclude instructor bikes.
fix: Check each of the eight daytime slots separately in case noon is packed.
Exclude off-peak daytime classes from the crowding audit completely.
Cut four empty daytime classes and move those instructors to 7 p.m.
Report the peak daytime class size alongside the 5-rider average.

diagnosis: Two 7 p.m. classes with 30 riders each is only 20% of the daily schedule, so it's a minor edge case.
30 riders at 7 p.m. is only crowded if the studio has fewer than 30 bikes.
Having two classes at 7 p.m. means 30 riders are split 15 per room, not 30 in one room.
Without knowing how many people got turned away at 7 p.m., 30 riders understates true evening demand.
fix: Report the studio's bike capacity alongside the 30-rider count.
Track evening waitlist turn-aways on top of the 30 riders who got in.
Clarify whether the two 7 p.m. classes run in two separate rooms of 30 each.
Compare 30 riders against the 5-rider daytime average as a 6× peak ratio.

diagnosis: A waiting-list reminder doesn't shrink the 30-person crowd — it just confirms evening slots are jammed.
Keeping the timetable unchanged wastes instructor pay on eight nearly empty daytime classes.
Adding a waiting-list reminder only for evening slots is unfair to daytime members.
If the average class really is 10 people, you don't even need a waiting-list reminder at 7 p.m.
fix: Shift two daytime slots into 6 p.m. or 8 p.m. evening classes to relieve the 60 evening riders.
Cap evening classes at 20 bikes and add a third evening session.
Keep the timetable unchanged and drop the waiting-list reminder too.
Offer a daytime discount to nudge evening riders into the 5-person slots.
